opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really welcome development, and frankly an overdue one. For a long time, screening of synthetic DNA orders has been largely voluntary. A number of the major providers, many of them through the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, have been screening sequences and customers for years, and they deserve real credit for that. But voluntary measures only go so far. If screening is optional, you're relying on the goodwill of every provider in the market, and it only takes one company that doesn't screen, perhaps because it's cheaper or faster not to, for someone with bad intentions to route around the whole system.

So moving toward a mandatory baseline closes that gap. It also levels the playing field commercially. Right now, companies that invest in screening are bearing a cost their competitors may not be. A requirement makes screening part of the cost of doing business rather than a competitive disadvantage.

That said, I'd add a few caveats. First, this is fundamentally a global problem. DNA synthesis is an international market, and a requirement in one country can push orders to providers elsewhere. Ideally we want harmonized standards across jurisdictions, or at least mutual recognition, so there aren't obvious weak links.

Second, we have to think about where the technology is going. Benchtop synthesizers are getting more capable, and if people can print DNA in their own labs, screening at the point of a commercial order becomes less of a chokepoint. Any serious framework needs to address those devices, for example by building screening into the machines themselves.

Third, the screening itself has to keep improving. Matching against lists of known pathogen sequences is a good start, but advances in AI-enabled biological design mean we may see sequences that are functionally dangerous without closely resembling anything on a list. So we need function-based approaches, regularly updated databases, and good customer verification, not just sequence matching.

And finally, it has to be done in a way that doesn't strangle legitimate research. The vast majority of people ordering DNA are doing valuable work: vaccines, diagnostics, basic science. The goal is a system that is fast, cheap, and low-friction for them, while making it meaningfully harder for the rare malicious actor. If we get that balance right, mandatory screening is one of the most cost-effective biosecurity measures we have.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. On the mandatory screening question, I'll give you my view at the level of policy design rather than technical specifics.

I think the movement is directionally right. Voluntary frameworks have done real good, and the firms that adopted them deserve credit, but voluntary regimes share a structural weakness: they bind the conscientious and leave everyone else untouched. That asymmetry gets worse as the supplier base grows and diversifies internationally. So a baseline obligation makes sense, both to close that gap and to remove the competitive penalty for providers who screen properly.

The harder part is implementation, and that's where I'd focus attention:

- **Who is covered.** Commercial providers are the easy case. Academic core facilities, small startups, and emerging suppliers outside the current consortium are where the real coverage questions sit.
- **What counts as compliance.** If every jurisdiction writes its own standard, you get fragmentation and cost without much added security. Harmonized expectations across the major synthesis markets matter more than any single country's rule being strict.
- **Verification and accountability.** A mandate with no auditing is a paperwork exercise. It needs some mechanism for checking that screening actually happens.
- **Legitimate research burden.** Researchers with entirely ordinary needs shouldn't face long delays or opaque denials. If the process feels arbitrary, you create pressure to route around it, which undermines the whole point.

My bigger worry is that mandatory screening becomes treated as the solution rather than one layer of several. It's a meaningful control, but it sits alongside institutional oversight, equipment governance, and norms within the research community. A mandate that's well designed and genuinely enforced is worth a great deal. One that's announced and then left to drift mostly buys reassurance, and reassurance isn't security.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very welcome development. Screening has, for a long time, depended on companies voluntarily doing the right thing. And that creates a problem: the companies investing in screening bear a cost that their competitors can avoid. Making it mandatory establishes a baseline and makes safety a shared responsibility.

But the details matter enormously. What do you screen for? How do you assess who the customer is? What happens when an order raises a concern? A requirement to screen isn’t necessarily a requirement to screen effectively. You need standards that can evolve as the technology changes, and some way of checking that those standards are actually being met.

You also want to make compliance straightforward and affordable, especially for smaller providers, while keeping legitimate research accessible. And because synthesis is an international market, coordination matters. The aim should be to make effective screening the normal way of doing business, rather than something a customer can simply avoid by ordering elsewhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very welcome development. Screening synthetic DNA and RNA is one of the practical things we can do to make it harder for someone to acquire the materials needed to create a dangerous pathogen. But if screening is voluntary, you’re relying on every provider choosing to participate, even when doing so costs money and takes time. That leaves gaps and puts responsible companies at a disadvantage.

Making it mandatory can establish a common baseline. The important question then is what that requirement actually means: which sequences are screened, how customers are verified, and what happens when an order raises a concern. A requirement needs to be backed by effective implementation, rather than becoming a box-ticking exercise.

And this is an international market. If you introduce strong requirements in one country but can simply order from a supplier elsewhere, you haven’t fully addressed the problem. So I’m encouraged by the direction of travel, but we need international coordination and screening that remains accessible to legitimate researchers. It’s an important layer of protection, rather than a complete solution to biological risk.
